body:
Noticed while canarying #263's dedup.

`data/normalized_yaml/algae/sbbm.yaml` carried this as an ingredient row:

```yaml
- preferred_term: Make up to 1 litre with distilled water. For agar add
  concentration:
    value: '15'
    unit: G_PER_L
  source: CCAP Medium MR_SBBM.pdf
```

That is a preparation instruction from the source PDF, parsed as an ingredient and given
the concentration of whatever followed it (the 15 g/l is presumably the agar). It appeared
twice, which is how the dedup pass surfaced it.

Two distinct harms:

1. **A phantom ingredient.** Anything counting ingredients, exporting to KG-Microbe, or
   computing composition sees a component that does not exist.
2. **A misattributed concentration.** If the 15 g/l belongs to agar, then agar is either
   missing its concentration or carrying a different one — worth checking which.

This is likely not one record. Candidate detection: `preferred_term` containing a verb
phrase, sentence punctuation, or exceeding some length — real ingredient names are short
noun phrases. A quick scan for `preferred_term` values containing `. ` or more than ~6
words would size it.

Related: #265 (ingredient synonyms effectively unpopulated) and #259 (`term.label` carrying
ingredient strings) are both symptoms of the same underlying thing — the ingredient field
is absorbing text it was not meant to hold.

comments.body:
**Do not implement this as a deletion — I checked, and it would lose real ingredient data.**

Scoping it properly. A conservative pattern (imperative volume/pH/dissolution phrases only,
excluding chemical formula notation like `MgSO4 . 7H2O` and genuine ingredients like
`Sterile Defibrinated Rabbit Blood`) finds **86 rows across 22 distinct strings**.

**All 86 carry a concentration.** That is the important part, and it is not incidental — it
confirms the parser attached the *following* ingredient's quantity to the instruction text.

`data/normalized_yaml/algae/sbbm.yaml` in full:

| preferred_term | value |
|---|---|
| `Make up to 1 litre with distilled water. For agar add` | 15 G_PER_L |
| `Add to 1000 ml of distilled water` | 0.75 G_PER_L |
| FeCl3 x 6 H2O | 0.097 |
| … | |
| `Soil is prepared as above.` | 105 G_PER_L |

**There is no separate agar ingredient in that record.** The 15 g/l agar exists *only* on
the instruction row. Deleting the row deletes the agar. Same for the 0.75 g/l on
`Add to 1000 ml of distilled water`, and the 105 g/l on `Soil is prepared as above.`

So the original framing here — "a phantom ingredient, remove it" — is wrong. These rows are
**mis-parsed but load-bearing**: the text is wrong, the quantity is real.

The actual fix is recovery, not deletion, and it is per-pattern:

- `... For agar add` @ 15 g/l → an `Agar` ingredient at 15 g/l. The substance is named in
  the text; this is recoverable, not guesswork.
- `Add to 1000 ml of distilled water` @ 0.75 g/l → the substance is *not* named. Needs the
  source PDF, or the value moves to a note flagged as unattributed.
- `Soil is prepared as above.` @ 105 g/l → likewise.

Suggested order:
1. Recover the cases where the text names the substance (`For agar add`, `For X add`).
2. For the rest, move text **and value** into a note marked as an unattributed quantity, so
   nothing is silently dropped and a curator can reattach from the source.
3. Only then consider whether the ingest parser can be fixed at source, which is the real
   cure — `create-recipe` / the CCAP PDF path is producing these.

I opened a branch for this and abandoned it rather than ship a deletion that loses data.

Found while reviewing the KGX export (#294 / PR #295): **this defect is on the `solutions` side too, not just `ingredients`.**

The longest minted node id in the whole corpus turns out to be a preparation protocol sitting in a solution `preferred_term`:

```
culturemech:solution_MgSO4·7H2O0.5gNH42SO40.4gK2HPO40.2gKCl0.1gDistilled_water1L
Adjust_pH_to_2.0_with_H2SO4.Heterotrophic_growth_on_yeast_extract_Add_10_mg_l_of
_FeSO4·7H2O_to_the_medium._After_autoclaving,_add_yeast_extract_from_sterile_
stock_solution_to_final_concentration_of_0.25_g_l.Autotrophic_growth_on_ferrous_
sulfate_Add_13.9_g_l_of_FeSO4·7H2O_to_the_medium,_and_adjust_medium_pH_to_1.7_
with_H2SO4prior_to_autoclaving.
```

Same shape as the `sbbm.yaml` case in the issue description — a chunk of source-PDF prose absorbed into a field meant for a short noun phrase — and it produces the same two harms, now demonstrably: a phantom solution node in the KGX export, and a `has_part` edge hanging off it.

Two things this suggests for the detection sweep proposed in the issue:

1. **Scan `solutions[].preferred_term` as well as `ingredients[].preferred_term`.** The heuristics named in the issue (sentence punctuation, verb phrase, more than ~6 words) apply unchanged; only the field list needs widening.
2. **Length alone finds the worst ones cheaply.** This value is several hundred characters. A simple `len(preferred_term) > 80` pass would size the tail before any linguistic heuristic is written.

Also worth noting the reverse direction: several solution names are bare section labels like `Solution A:`, `Solution B:` — the opposite failure, where the field holds a document structure marker rather than a substance. Those are real rows in the corpus too (19 ids carried a trailing colon before PR #295 stripped it).

Not fixing any of this in #295 — that PR only makes the export run and be internally consistent. But the export now provides a cheap way to *see* these: `just kgx-export-sample <category>` renders the parsed field values as node names in one TSV, which is how this one surfaced.

Sized this against the now-runnable KGX export (#294/#295), and one thing in my earlier comment needs correcting.

**Correction: these phantom ingredients do NOT reach the KGX export.** I previously listed #273 as putting phantom nodes and edges into the graph. That is wrong. `medium_to_ingredient_edge` returns `None` without a `term.id`, and every one of the 44 high-confidence phantom rows is ungrounded (44/44). Measured on the full export:

```
$ grep -c Make_up_to_1_litre culturemech_nodes.tsv culturemech_edges.tsv
nodes: 0
edges: 0
```

So the harm is the one the issue states first — ingredient counts, composition analysis, and anything reading the corpus directly — not the KG. That lowers its KGX-criticality relative to what I said; it does not lower its data-quality severity.

## Sizing

Over all 15,877 records: 169,418 ingredient values and 5,949 solution values.

| filter | ingredients | solutions |
|---|---:|---:|
| any flag (len>80 / sentence / >6 words / instruction verb) | 1,192 | 377 |
| high confidence (instruction verb AND long-or-sentence) | 44 | 29 |

The high-confidence ingredient set is tightly clustered — 29 of the 44 are one of about 7 CCAP phrasings:

```
x6  "Make up to 1 litre with deionised water. For agar, add"                                conc 15 G_PER_L
x6  "Make up to 1 litre with filtered natural seawater. Adjust pH to 8.0 with"              conc 1 MOLAR
x3  "Add the above constituents and make up to 1 litre with deionised water. For agar, add" conc 15 G_PER_L
x2  "Make up to 1 litre with deionised water. Adjust pH to 7-8 with"                        conc 1 MOLAR
x2  "Make up to 1 litre with distilled water. For agar add"                                 conc 15 G_PER_L
```

The concentration attached to each is exactly the misattribution the issue predicted: `15 G_PER_L` is the agar that followed "For agar, add", and `1 MOLAR` is the acid or base that followed "Adjust pH to X with". So the repair is two-part per row — drop the phantom, and check whether the trailing ingredient it stole from is missing its value.

## Two things to widen in the detection sweep

1. **Scan `solutions[].preferred_term` too** — 29 high-confidence hits there.
2. **`len(preferred_term) > 80` is the cheapest first pass** and finds the worst tail with no linguistic heuristic.

## Split out: #299

The solution-side hits are mostly *not* this defect. They are whole composition tables concatenated into one string with `composition: []`, and in those records the chemical name has landed in `concentration.value` with an empty `preferred_term` (59 rows). That is an importer failure rather than prose leakage, and unlike this issue it **does** reach the export (54 nodes, 86 edges). Filed separately so the two do not get one fix.

title: Preparation instructions are parsed as ingredients with concentrations
